newsitem.title: DUBAI: Dubai traders feel pinch of Iran-Afghan row.
newsitem.headline: Dubai traders feel pinch of Iran-Afghan row.

text.p: Traders in Dubai said on Tuesday they feared their booming business with Afghanistan could fall victim to rifts between Iran and Afghanistan's Islamist Taleban militia.

"The short term impact of Iran's move on Sunday to halt Afghan transit trade could be losses in millions of dollars to Dubai traders who deal with Afghanistan," a Dubai trader who refused to be named told Reuters.

Dubai, a major regional re-export and trading centre, is source to many of the electronic and household goods imported by Afghanistan, which has no import restrictions. Dubai traders said most goods were then smuggled to Pakistan.
The goods reach Afghanistan via Iran across the Gulf from Dubai, one of the seven emirates of the United Arab Emirates.

The trader said about 80 Dubai-based companies, most trading with Afghanistan since the 1970s, have over 400 containers stranded at the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas since Iran -- apparently angered by the Islamic Taleban militia's closure of its embassy in Kabul -- closed the transit trade through the Afghan border city of Islam Qila on Sunday.
The Taleban ordered the Iranian embassy in Kabul to close last week and expelled its staff, saying they had been interfering in Afghanistan's internal affairs -- a charge Iran denies.
The cross-border trade from Iran has been one of the Taleban's main sources of revenue.
Dubai traders -- who could not give a figure for the value of their trade with Afghanistan -- said over 1,000 containers from other countries were also held up at the Iranian port.
"My firm has 28 containers loaded with about $800,000 worth of electronics, textiles, foodstuffs and plastics," one said.
"Unless Tehran decides to clear goods which arrived at Bandar Abbas before the closure, we will have to make arrangments to ship the containers back to Dubai," he added.
Another Dubai trader said alternative routes would be expensive and slow. Traders said other routes could cost about four times more per container than about the $1,000 cost through Iran.
"While it takes five days now for shipments to reach Afganistan, they could take up to three months through Siberia," he added.
The traders said they plan to meet on Wednesday to request that the UAE government intervene with Iran to lift the ban on transit trade.
"The goods were destined to a war-torn Islamic country in need of food," said one trader. "Iran is an Islamic country and should facilitate the flow of goods to another brotherly Islamic country."
